records.toxicity_detail: This species' hazard is a contact-dermatitis one, not an ingestion toxin, and that distinction is confirmed by the sources themselves. All parts of the plant -- bark, flowers, fruits, leaves, roots, sap/juice, seeds, and stems, including aerial roots -- contain urushiol, an oily resin; NC State Extension rates human Poison Severity as "High," names the toxic principle as "Urushiol," and confirms "Causes Contact Dermatitis: Yes," with skin contact or inhaled smoke producing "inflammation, itching, and blistering" that is "significant and long-lasting for most humans." UF/IFAS independently confirms urushiol "is present in all parts of the plants, including its aerial roots, dried leaves, and fruits." This is distinct from ingestion toxicity to pets: NC State's own structured pet-safety tags mark the species non-toxic for cats, dogs, and horses -- pets are not poisoned by the plant. However, urushiol transfers readily by indirect contact and persists for months on surfaces, including animal fur. UF/IFAS states the allergic reaction "can also occur indirectly if the oil has been in contact with an animal, tools, clothes, or shoes." Clemson, Penn State, University of Maryland, and UGA Extension each independently confirm that dogs and cats can carry the oil on their coats and transfer it to a person who touches them: Clemson and UMD both state "The rash can be picked up on tools, clothing, and the fur of pets" and that the oil "can remain active for months on objects"; Penn State states "The liquid can get on tools, pets, or clothing, and when you touch them, you can pick it up"; and UGA states "Dogs and cats also frequently transfer the toxin to people."

records.name_note: No accepted-name conflict among admissible sources: NC State's structured Attributes block reads "Genus: Phytolacca Species: americana Family: Phytolaccaceae," and RHS's Name Status field for Phytolacca americana reads "Correct." RHS separately lists Phytolacca decandra as a synonym ("Synonyms Phytolacca decandra"), which no source disputes or elevates as an alternate accepted name. NC State also documents a distinct coastal variety, Phytolacca americana var. rigida, as more severely toxic than the species generally ("is highly toxic and may be fatal if eaten"); this record covers the species Phytolacca americana as such, not that variety, and the var. rigida distinction is noted here only for completeness.
records.toxicity_detail: All parts of the plant are treated as poisonous. NC State Extension states plainly that "all parts of this plant are poisonous to humans and pets," and UF/IFAS EDIS (AG254) reports that all parts contain saponins, oxalates, and the alkaloid phytolacine, with the roots and seeds carrying the highest concentrations. UF/IFAS EDIS (EP631) names dogs specifically among the animals it is "largely toxic" to, alongside cattle, sheep, poultry, horses, and humans, and states that ingestion "can even cause death in rare cases" depending on the quantity consumed; RHS separately flags it as "Harmful to pets if eaten (dogs)" and advises wearing gloves when handling. No admissible source names cats specifically -- only dogs (RHS, UF/IFAS) and a generic "pets" (NC State) are given. NC State's own detailed Poison block (Severity: Medium; specific diarrhea/vomiting/chromosome-damage symptoms) is explicitly headed "Poisonous to Humans:" on the source page, so those specifics are not carried over here as pet-toxicity data -- only the separate, unheaded sentence naming pets was used for that purpose. A well-documented regional folk tradition (poke sallet) uses only the young spring shoots and leaves, and only after they are boiled in at least two changes of water with the water discarded each time (Missouri Botanical Garden; UF/IFAS AG254, which adds an unconfirmed "some say" claim that a further boiling removes essentially all toxins). This preparation-dependent exception is documented for human consumption of young shoots only: it does not extend to mature leaves, fruit, seeds, or roots (the most toxic parts), it is not addressed at all in the pet-toxicity sources above, and it is not treated here as evidence of general safety. Penn State Extension, in contrast, states without any preparation exception that "new leaves and roots, along with the berries, should not be eaten because they are toxic."

UGA's toxicity table entry lumps Lonicera japonica together with Lonicera sempervirens (Trumpet Honeysuckle) into one combined row rather than giving L. japonica its own line, so its species-specific weight is softer than NC State's dedicated single-species entry.

Invasive-species status (flagged per task instructions; the schema has no dedicated field for it): nearly every admissible source calls this species invasive. NC State: 'This plant is an invasive species in North Carolina.' Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder (plantfinder.mobot.org, taxonid=245393, 'Halliana'): 'This vine can be quite invasive, and can rapidly cover and literally suffocate shrubs or small trees if allowed to climb on them. Not recommended. It is a dreadful weed.' Penn State Extension's dedicated article is titled 'The Invasive Japanese Honeysuckle' (extension.psu.edu/the-invasive-japanese-honeysuckle) and describes it as displacing native species and strangling trees/shrubs/structures. University of Maryland Extension (extension.umd.edu/resource/japanese-honeysuckle): 'Do not plant Japanese honeysuckle, and replace existing specimens when possible.' RHS's own structured plant description states: 'This plant is listed as an invasive non-native species in Northern Ireland' and the species is on Schedule 9 of the UK Wildlife & Countryside Act (Northern Ireland), making it an offence to plant or cause it to grow in the wild there.

soil_base ('garden_bed') and soil_drainage ('moderate') are best-fit mappings rather than literal source vocabulary: the schema's soil_base enum is oriented toward container/potting substrates, but every admissible source describes L. japonica growing directly in outdoor garden soil (Clay/Loam/Sand per NC State; Clay/Loam, 'Moist but well-drained' per RHS), never in a pot or houseplant mix -- garden_bed/moderate are the closest defensible values given that.

records.name_note: Cattleya is commonly sold and grown as a genus rather than one accepted species-level binomial -- admissible sources default to genus-level treatment. NC State Extension's own top-level page for this plant is a genus overview titled "Cattleya" (common names "Brazilian Orchid, Cat Orchid, Corsage Orchid, Queen of orchids"), distinct from -- and broader than -- its individual species pages for Cattleya mossiae, Cattleya trianae, Cattleya forbesii, and Cattleya labiata; no admissible source frames any one of these species as "the" Cattleya orchid the way Phalaenopsis is dominated by one hybrid complex. Missouri Botanical Garden's own care page and Plant Finder entry likewise group the plant as "Cattleya" / "Cattleya (group)" rather than a single species, and RHS's genus-level details page ("Cattleya | RHS") covers the genus with its own structured description ("A genus of tropical orchids native to South and Central America...") and no single accepted species named as primary. Given this, scientific_name_given is recorded as the genus "Cattleya" rather than forced to one binomial, following the same genus-level pattern used for Water Lily (Nymphaea) elsewhere in this catalog. scientific_name_accepted is likewise recorded as "Cattleya": unlike the Water Lily case, RHS's genus-level page here carries its own explicit structured taxonomy verdict for the genus name itself -- "Name Status: Correct" -- so the genus name is recorded as accepted rather than left null.
records.cool_rest_note: Sources disagree on the minimum safe night temperature specific to this genus. NC State Extension and Missouri Botanical Garden both state Cattleya's night temperature range bottoms out at 55 degrees F ("55 to 60 degrees F at night"), while Clemson Cooperative Extension's orchid genus-comparison table recommends a higher minimum specifically for cattleya: "The minimum night temperature recommended for phalaenopsis is 65 °F; cattleya, 60 °F; and dendrobium, 52 °F." Because these give different floors for the same genus, chill_damage_f is left null rather than set to either 55°F or 60°F; treat 60°F as Clemson's recommended protective minimum and 55°F as NC State/MOBOT's stated comfortable-range floor.

records.water_estimate_basis: Missouri Botanical Garden: "Mature Cattleyas should be watered thoroughly about once a week or more with lukewarm water" -- the literal "once a week" floor is recorded as 7 days; the "or more" allowance is not captured as a separate numeric value.
unknowns: chill_damage_f: left null -- a genuine conflict on a harm-capable field. NC State and MOBOT state Cattleya's comfortable night range bottoms out at 55F, while Clemson's genus-comparison table recommends a higher protective minimum of 60F specifically for cattleya. Both figures are captured, correctly attributed, in cool_rest_note instead of picking one.

direct_sun_hours_max: left null. records.name_note: Matricaria chamomilla is the currently accepted name: RHS lists "Name Status: Correct" for Matricaria chamomilla and "Name Status: Synonym" for Matricaria recutita. NC State Extension's Plant Toolbox (titled "German Chamomile - Matricaria chamomilla") lists "Previously known as: Chamomilla recutita, Matricaria recutita," agreeing with RHS. Missouri Botanical Garden's Plant Finder catalogs the same plant under the name Matricaria recutita as its database entry point without making an explicit accepted/synonym determination, but its description, uses, and common names are unambiguously the same species. This record covers German chamomile specifically, not the unrelated Roman chamomile (Chamaemelum nobile, a perennial groundcover commonly sold interchangeably as "chamomile"): NC State explicitly flags that Matricaria chamomilla "is often confused with: Chamaemelum nobile," and Clemson HGIC's herb factsheet separates the two species by name and growth habit side by side. Every citation below was checked to confirm it specifically discusses Matricaria chamomilla/recutita and not Chamaemelum nobile.
unknowns: direct_sun_hours_max null: NC State gives the full-sun threshold as '6 or more hours' but no admissible source states an upper bound on tolerated direct-sun hours.

soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max null: RHS's structured pH field for this species reads 'Acid, Alkaline, or Neutral' (i.e. broad tolerance across all categories), not a numeric range, and no other admissible source states a pH value.

Neither wording maps cleanly onto this catalog's four water-regime categories without inventing an interpretation, so it is left null rather than guessed.

Partial Shade'), Missouri Botanical Garden ('Sun: Full sun'), and Clemson HGIC ('in sun or part shade') -- all independently agree on full sun to part shade for German chamomile specifically, with none supporting full shade. Given this, full_sun and part_shade are used and full_shade is treated as an outlier contradicted by the source's own prose and by every other admissible source.

normalizations: 2026-08-23: twelfth batch of the "blind spots" pass. Poison Ivy is a genuinely new case for this catalog -- its hazard is contact dermatitis (urushiol), not ingestion, the first plant landed with that distinction. toxic_to_pets is correctly false (pets aren't poisoned by it) while toxicity_detail captures the real, well-documented risk that pets carry urushiol on their fur and transfer it to the humans who pet them -- a nuance five independent sources (Clemson, Penn State, UMD, UGA, UF/IFAS) converge on. Pokeweed confirmed toxic_to_pets=true (phytolaccatoxin, despite a folk food tradition of eating young shoots after extensive preparation, which the record correctly declined to read as a safety signal). Rounded out with Bald Cypress (completing a "wet-tolerant tree" trio alongside River Birch and Sycamore, both already in this catalog, all three named together in the same UMD source), Japanese Honeysuckle, Trumpet Vine, Hens and Chicks, a Cattleya orchid, and German Chamomile.

Trumpet Vine's toxic_to_pets was correctly nulled after the audit found the record's sole support was RHS's generic ornamental-fruit "not to be eaten" advisory boilerplate, which never uses the words toxic/poisonous/harmful and is applied broadly regardless of actual toxicity -- a good example of the catalog's discipline against reading routine handling caution as a toxicity finding.

One landing-time repair: Cattleya's common_name was nulled because "Cattleya Orchid" was a constructed label, not a name any source actually used -- restored as "Brazilian Orchid", the first of NC State's own listed common names, already directly quoted in an existing citation in this same record.

One defect this batch's own audit missed and this landing pass caught independently: Cattleya's water_growing_days_est=7 had no citation with a matching claim label anywhere in the record -- the quote it was supposedly derived from (MOBOT's 'about once a week or more') was never actually added to the citations array. Nulled to match this catalog's consistent standard.
